newsitem.title: USA: Snow Birds don't escape finances with trek to South.
newsitem.headline: Snow Birds don't escape finances with trek to South.

text.p: It's the time of year when many northern retirees start to pack up their belongings and head south for the winter.
It's nice to follow the endless summer, but these "snowbirds" are not as free as the migratory birds for which they are named.
Birds, for example, don't have to worry about frozen pipes and bills that follow them in their north-to-south flight formations.

The dual-household lifestyle carries with it many financial complications from the mundane, like the question of how to keep up with bills when you aren't around for six months, to the more serious. For example, which state do you really live in?

If you're ready to say goodbye to snow, but not ready to give up your northern residence, here are some financial questions to consider and some savings tips that might even help finance the migration.

-- Pay your bills in advance before you go. This advice may sound contradictory to traditional cash flow management, but if you are used to paying a $30 electric bill every month, you can just send the electric company a check for $180.

Then you won't have to worry about keeping up with your electric bill for six months. Worried about losing the interest? If you kept $180 in your checking account for six months, you're likely to earn about $2.50 in interest. That's not even enough to cover the stamps and envelopes you'd buy to mail in those six payments.

-- Get electric. The more computer literate you are, the easier it is to change venue all the time. You can dial in your brokerage account from either address and look at a statement, "talk" to your kids online without paying long distance charges, or authorise electronic payment of your bills.

-- Check your health insurance. Is your medigap policy through an HMO that's a lot better in one location than another? Or not available nationally? You may have to switch to find one that is just as good in Florida as it is in New York.

-- You might get a break on your car insurance. If you migrate from a high-rate northern state to a less dense southern one, you might be able to cut your car insurance costs by telling your insurer. Lewis Altfest, a New York financial planner with several "snowbird" clients, says he knows of one who buys a six month auto policy every time he goes south, and switches it on his return north.

-- Consider your residency carefully, suggests financial planner Deena Katz. If you become a permanent Florida resident, you won't have to pay state income taxes, but you will have to pay a small tax on your financial assets.

On the other hand, if you stay a New York resident (to choose an example) you might get a tax credit for much of your pension income and find an easier eventual path toward qualifying for Medicaid, should you need long term nursing home care. It can help to hire an accountant just to help you decide where you're better off being a full time resident. If you change your legal residency, you may have to spend money re-registering your car.

-- Think about clever ways of financing the winter home. Another Altfest scenario: If you intend to leave money to your kids anyway, consider giving them enough money ($20,000 a year for each kid from you and your spouse is the tax free limit) to buy your Florida home. Then they can rent it to you.

They can get tax writeoffs for the cost of carrying the rental property (including their trips down to check on their properties during Spring Break). You don't get much out of this arrangement, unless you are worried about having so much money you're trying to get out of estate taxes, or unless you are financially and personally secure enough that you enjoy giving your kids very expensive presents.

-- Be creative about where you migrate. You can save as much as 20 percent on your winter retirement home if you're willing to go to central Florida instead of southern Florida, reports Katz. You can save even more if you find a place in Alabama or Texas that you like.

-- If you are a renter, keep a post office box up down south. Then you don't have to worry about constantly shifting addresses. Have the post office up north forward your mail to your southern address, without changing your address with all of your contacts.
-- Forget about subscribing to magazines; too stressful when you lose a couple of months every year as your address changes catch up with you.
-- Get your northern doctors to recommend qualified southern professionals.

-- Spend money getting help. Have professionals pack and ship most of your stuff, pay neighbours to look after the home that's empty half a year, take Amtrak's auto train south, or hire students to drive the car down while you fly. All of these cut your stress level and remember, it's supposed to be a vacation!
